title: Principles of Emergency and Disaster Care
path: Concepts and Principles of Emergency Care
Principles of Emergency and Disaster Care

headings.title: Introduction to Emergency and Disaster Nursing
headings.content: Emergency and disaster nursing is a specialized, fast-paced field that requires nurses to think critically, act decisively, and manage acute crises under immense pressure. In the context of Nigeria's healthcare system, emergency nurses often encounter resource-limited settings where they must prioritize care for trauma victims, infectious disease outbreaks, and mass casualty events like road traffic accidents or structural collapses. The primary goal of emergency nursing is to rapidly identify life-threatening conditions, stabilize patients, and prevent further injury or death. Nurses in this field must possess advanced clinical competencies, emotional resilience, and the ability to adapt to chaotic environments. Furthermore, understanding the legal and professional frameworks guiding emergency care in Nigeria ensures that nurses operate safely within their scope of practice while upholding patient advocacy. Preparation involves continuous training in basic and advanced life support, triage systems, and effective communication with multidisciplinary teams including paramedics, physicians, and community leaders. Ultimately, emergency nursing bridges the gap between pre-hospital care and definitive medical or surgical intervention, serving as a critical pillar in safeguarding public health during sudden health crises.

headings.title: Core Principles and Ethics of Emergency Care
headings.content: Core principles and ethics in emergency care guide nurses in making swift, morally sound decisions during high-stress situations. Unlike routine clinical care where informed consent and thorough planning are standard, emergency care is frequently governed by the principle of implied consent when a patient is unconscious or incapacitated. Nurses must prioritize care based on clinical acuity rather than social status, wealth, or background, adhering strictly to the ethical principle of justice. Beneficence—acting in the best interest of the patient—and non-maleficence—doing no harm—are equally paramount when interventions must be executed rapidly. In disaster settings where resources are severely strained, nurses may face harrowing ethical dilemmas regarding resource allocation, requiring a shift from individual-focused care to population-based utilitarian principles (doing the greatest good for the greatest number of people). Professional accountability demands that Nigerian nurses remain aware of their legal boundaries, document interventions accurately despite chaotic conditions, and advocate for vulnerable patients who cannot speak for themselves. Upholding these ethical standards preserves human dignity and professional integrity when the healthcare system is pushed to its absolute limits.

headings.title: The Disaster Management Cycle: Mitigation and Preparedness
headings.content: The disaster management cycle comprises distinct phases designed to minimize the impact of hazards and enhance community resilience. Mitigation and preparedness form the proactive foundation of this cycle, occurring long before a disaster strikes. Mitigation involves structural and non-structural measures aimed at reducing vulnerability to hazards, such as enforcing building codes in earthquake-prone regions or creating flood barriers in vulnerable Nigerian riverine communities. Preparedness focuses on readiness activities, including developing comprehensive disaster response plans, conducting simulation drills, stockpiling essential medical supplies, and educating the public on safety measures. For student nurses, understanding these phases is crucial because healthcare facilities must be operationally ready to surge their capacity at a moment's notice. Preparedness also involves establishing reliable communication channels and clarifying roles within the interprofessional healthcare team. By engaging in mitigation and preparedness, nursing personnel help bridge community vulnerabilities with robust healthcare responses, ultimately saving lives and reducing economic losses when disasters materialize.

headings.title: Triage Principles in Mass Casualty Incidents
headings.content: Triage is the sorting of patients based on the severity of their injuries to maximize the number of survivors when medical resources are overwhelmed by mass casualty incidents (MCIs). In disaster nursing, the standard triage system frequently utilized is the Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment (START) method, which assesses respiration, perfusion, and mental status (RPM) in under 60 seconds per patient. Triage categories are universally color-coded: Red represents immediate life-threatening conditions requiring urgent intervention; Yellow indicates delayed care for serious injuries that are currently stable; Green denotes minor injuries ('walking wounded'); and Black (or Expectant) is assigned to deceased or mortally wounded individuals whose injuries are incompatible with survival given available resources. In resource-limited settings across Nigeria, nurses must remain calm and objective during triage, resisting the urge to provide prolonged individual care to red-tagged patients at the expense of others who could be saved. Accurate triage prevents chaos in the emergency department and ensures that critical interventions are delivered to those with the highest chance of survival.

headings.title: Rapid Primary and Secondary Patient Assessment
headings.content: Rapid patient assessment in emergency and disaster nursing relies on a systematic approach to identify and manage life threats immediately. The foundational framework is the primary survey, structured around the ABCDE mnemonic: Airway (with cervical spine protection), Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure. Any compromise found in the primary survey must be addressed immediately before moving to the next step. For instance, if an obstructed airway is identified, it must be cleared instantly. Once the patient is stabilized and immediate life threats are controlled, the nurse performs a secondary survey. This is a head-to-toe clinical evaluation that includes obtaining a detailed medical history using the SAMPLE mnemonic (Signs/symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last oral intake, Events leading to the incident), conducting a thorough physical examination, and monitoring vital signs. In emergency departments and disaster zones in Nigeria, mastering both primary and secondary surveys allows nurses to work efficiently, communicate effectively with medical teams, and detect hidden injuries that could deteriorate a patient's condition.

headings.title: Emergency Resuscitation and Life Support Guidelines
headings.content: Emergency resuscitation and life support guidelines provide standardized protocols for managing cardiac arrest, severe respiratory failure, and traumatic shock. Basic Life Support (BLS) focuses on early recognition of cardiac arrest, prompt activation of emergency response systems, high-quality chest compressions, and early defibrillation using an Automated External Defibrillator (AED). Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) builds upon BLS by incorporating advanced airway management, intravenous or intraosseous vascular access, administration of emergency cardiac medications like epinephrine, and identifying reversible causes of arrest (the H's and T's). In trauma scenarios, adherence to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) principles ensures aggressive fluid resuscitation, hemorrhage control, and prevention of the lethal triad: hypothermia, coagulopathy, and metabolic acidosis. Nursing students must be proficient in delivering effective chest compressions, managing bag-valve-mask ventilation, and operating monitoring equipment. Timely and coordinated resuscitation efforts significantly improve survival rates and neurological outcomes for patients facing critical physiological collapse in Nigerian hospitals and pre-hospital environments.

headings.title: Disaster Response and Incident Command Systems
headings.content: Disaster response requires a coordinated multi-agency approach to prevent chaos and ensure resources are deployed efficiently. The Incident Command System (ICS) is a standardized, on-scene management framework designed to integrate facilities, equipment, personnel, procedures, and communications under a unified structure. ICS establishes a clear chain of command, designating an Incident Commander who oversees operational sections such as operations, planning, logistics, and finance/administration. In Nigerian disaster management, nurses often operate within the medical or health branch of the ICS structure, collaborating seamlessly with fire services, police, civil defense, and public health officials. Effective communication protocols, such as using plain language instead of internal jargon and establishing redundant communication lines, prevent misunderstandings during high-stress operations. Understanding the Incident Command System enables nursing professionals to know their reporting lines, maintain situational awareness, and contribute effectively to large-scale disaster mitigation and patient rescue operations without duplicating efforts.

headings.title: Post-Disaster Recovery, Evaluation, and Psychosocial Support
headings.content: The post-disaster phase focuses on recovery, evaluation, and providing vital psychosocial support to affected populations and healthcare workers alike. Recovery involves transitioning from emergency operations back to community stabilization, repairing damaged infrastructure, restoring health services, and evaluating the effectiveness of the disaster response through debriefings and after-action reviews. Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) and psychological first aid (PFA) are essential components of post-disaster care, addressing trauma, grief, and acute stress disorders among survivors and healthcare staff. Nurses play a frontline role in delivering empathetic psychosocial support, active listening, and early identification of mental health disturbances such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression. In Nigeria, where disasters like flooding, communal clashes, and epidemics frequently leave lasting psychological scars, culturally sensitive mental health nursing is vital for holistic recovery. Evaluating response gaps helps institutions improve preparedness plans for future events, ensuring continuous quality improvement in emergency nursing practice.
